Grade 3 · Unit 3.1

Forces, Motion, and Magnets

Why do objects speed up, slow down, turn, or stay still?

A force is a push or a pull. Forces explain why things speed up, slow down, turn or stay put. You will compare balanced and unbalanced forces, use patterns in motion to predict what happens next, explore magnets and static electricity that push and pull without touching, and design a way to move something using magnets.

In this lesson

  1. Balanced and unbalanced forces
  2. Motion patterns help predict
  3. Forces without touching
  4. Magnet design problem
  5. Try it at home or in class
  6. Check yourself
  7. Play: Magnet sandbox

Look for these tags: Diagram Try it Data Real world

Concept 1

Balanced and unbalanced forces

Balanced forces keep motion the same; unbalanced forces change motion. Equal pulls balance. Unequal pulls move the rope. Friction is a rubbing force that pushes against motion.

Try it

Fair tests and Claim, Evidence, Reasoning

You need: two toy cars, one ramp, and sentence cards labeled Claim, Evidence, and Reasoning.

“Change one thing at a time, like the ramp height. If we change the car and the ramp together, we do not know which one changed the distance.”

“Claim: What we think. Evidence: What we measured. Reasoning: Why it fits.”

You did this before. What is new: You used fair tests and Claim, Evidence, Reasoning cards in Unit 0. Now you use them to investigate forces.

Try it

Push the car

You need: a toy car and a table.

  • Push the car gently. Watch how far it goes.
  • Push it harder. Which push changed its motion more?

Extra: Flick a marble across a smooth tray and mark where it is every second.

What you should see: On a smooth tray, the distances between marks stay almost the same, so the motion hardly changes. On rough carpet the distances shrink quickly, because friction pushes against the motion.

You did this before. What is new: You pushed and pulled objects in K-A. Now you collect evidence about balanced and unbalanced forces.

Diagram

Force arrows

Force arrows show pushes and pulls. A longer arrow is a bigger push or pull. Equal arrows that point opposite ways cancel out, so nothing changes. Unequal arrows change the motion.

“Same-length arrows pointing opposite ways: no change. Different-length arrows: motion changes.”

Concept 2

Motion patterns help predict

If motion repeats, we can predict what happens next. Speed tells how fast something moves. Distance is how far it goes in a set time.

Try it

Rolling ball track

You need: a ball, a book to make a ramp, a tape measure, and masking tape.

  • Roll the ball down the ramp and across the floor.
  • Ask a grown-up to say “now” every second. At each “now,” tape a marker where the ball is.
  • Repeat three times. Look for the pattern.

You did this before. What is new: You moved objects in K-A. Now you use repeated motion to make a prediction.

Data

Real ball on a floor

Example data for a ball rolling across a real floor:

  • 0 s: 0 cm (about 0 in) from the start.
  • 1 s: 9 cm (about 3.5 in) from the start. It moved 9 cm (about 3.5 in) in that second.
  • 2 s: 16 cm (about 6 in) from the start. It moved 7 cm (about 3 in) in that second.
  • 3 s: 21 cm (about 8 in) from the start. It moved 5 cm (about 2 in) in that second.

“Short distances between marks mean slow. Long distances mean fast.”

Data

Model ball with no friction

A model ball ignores rubbing, so the distance it moves each second stays the same:

  • 0 s: 0 cm (about 0 in).
  • 1 s: 10 cm (about 4 in).
  • 2 s: 20 cm (about 8 in).
  • 3 s: 30 cm (about 12 in).
  • 4 s (prediction): 40 cm (about 16 in).

“The distance goes up by 10 cm every second. If the pattern keeps going, the ball will be 40 cm (about 16 inches) away at 4 seconds.”

Concept 3

Forces without touching

Magnets and static electricity can push or pull without direct touch. A magnet pulls on some metals, such as iron and steel, even from a short distance away. Static electricity is a charge that builds up on things like a rubbed balloon.

Try it

Force Track

Quick round, about 5 minutes. Push a box, roll a ball, and test a magnet on a few objects that do not touch it. Change one thing, predict, then test again.

Try it

Static demo

You need: a balloon, small paper bits, and (if you have a tray) a thin stream of water from a faucet.

  • Rub the balloon on your hair or a wool sweater.
  • Hold it near the paper bits. Watch them jump toward it.
  • Move the balloon farther away. What happens?

What you should see: The paper bits jump toward the balloon. Farther away, the pull gets weaker.

Safety: Do the water-stream demo over a tray, keep water away from Chromebooks, and dry your hands before touching a keyboard.

Diagram

Magnet field

A magnetic field is the space around a magnet where it can pull.

Red end: north (N). Blue end: south (S). The curved lines show the magnetic field.

Text version of this diagram

A bar magnet has a red north end on the left and a blue south end on the right. Curved lines loop from one end to the other, closest together at the ends. A paper clip near the north end is pulled toward the magnet.

“The force is strongest near the ends. It can pass through thin paper.”

Real world

Compass

The red end of the needle swings to point toward magnetic north.

“Earth acts like a giant magnet. A compass needle is a small magnet, and it lines up with Earth’s magnetism. Its red end points toward magnetic north.”

Concept 4

Magnet design problem

We can use magnet ideas to move something without touching it directly. A criterion is what success looks like. A constraint is a rule about what you may use.

Try it

Paper-clip mover

You need: a paper clip, an index card or thin cardboard, and one large ceramic or ferrite magnet.

“Move the clip without touching it. Plan. Test. Improve.”

Predict first: Will a magnet under the card still move the clip on top? How far apart can they be?

  1. Put the clip on the card. Hold the magnet under the card.
  2. Slide the magnet slowly. Watch the clip follow.
  3. Measure how far the clip travels. Is it 20 cm (about 8 inches) or more?
  4. Change one thing (thicker card, or a different path) and test again.

What you should see: A thinner card should let the magnet pull harder. Test it to check.

Why it matters: This is design: test, find what failed, change one thing, test again.

Diagram

Criteria and constraints

A criterion is what it must do: the clip moves at least 20 cm (about 8 inches) and no hand touches it. A constraint is what you must use: one magnet, one paper clip, and paper or card.

“Criterion: What it must do. Constraint: What you must use.”

Hands-on: design or investigate

Try it at home or in class

Design a paper-clip mover that moves a paper clip at least 20 cm (about 8 inches) without touching the clip directly. The criterion is that the clip moves the full distance. The constraints are one magnet, one paper clip, paper or card, and no direct touching. You test, record evidence, and improve your design.

Try it

What you need

  • Toy car
  • Cardboard ramp
  • Books
  • Tape
  • Small ball
  • Index cards
  • Pencil and paper
  • 2 large ceramic or ferrite magnets
  • Paper clips
  • Balloon
  • Small paper bits
  • String

Safety: Keep magnets away from Chromebooks and other electronics. Use only large ceramic or ferrite magnets; small, very strong magnets can be swallowed and are dangerous. Keep every magnet out of mouths. Do the water-stream static demo over a tray, keep water away from Chromebooks, and dry your hands before touching a keyboard.

Try it

What you do

  • Push a toy car gently, then harder. Say which push changed its motion more (10 minutes).
  • Roll a ball down a ramp and mark where it is each second. Draw the distances (10 minutes).
  • Test a magnet on a few objects. Write yes or no (10 minutes).
  • Do the balloon demo: rub it on your hair, then hold it over paper bits (5 minutes).
  • Design the paper-clip mover. Test, change one thing, and test again (20 minutes).

Notice: Short distances between marks mean slow. Long distances mean fast. A magnet and a charged balloon both act without touching.

Why it matters: Each step gives you evidence for balanced forces, patterns in motion, and pushes or pulls at a distance.

No time or no good weather? Use this data

This data is a backup. It lets you practice reading evidence, but collect your own when you can.

  • Model ball, no friction: 0, 10, 20, 30 cm (about 0, 4, 8, 12 in) at 0, 1, 2, 3 seconds. Predict 40 cm (about 16 in) at 4 seconds.
  • Real ball on carpet: 0, 9, 16, 21 cm (about 0, 3.5, 6, 8 in). The gaps are 9, 7 and 5 cm. Do not predict 40 cm. Predict a smaller gap each second.

A model with even gaps means balanced forces. A real ball on carpet has friction, so its gaps shrink. Notice this in your own data.

Near you: Michigan’s Upper Peninsula has a long history of iron mining. Iron is a metal that magnets pull on, but not all iron ore is strongly magnetic.

Check yourself

What did you learn?

0 of 4 correct

Words to know

  • Force: a push or a pull.
  • Balanced forces: forces that cancel out, so motion does not change.
  • Unbalanced forces: forces that change motion.
  • Motion: a change in position.
  • Pattern: something that repeats.
  • Friction: a rubbing force that pushes against motion.
  • Magnet: an object that attracts some metals, such as iron and steel.
  • Magnetic field: the space around a magnet where it can pull.
  • Attract: to pull toward.
  • Repel: to push away.
  • Static electricity: a charge that can make small objects move without touching.
  • Criterion: what success looks like.
  • Constraint: a rule about what you may use.
Tutor notes: misconceptions and pacing

Pacing: six 30-minute sessions.

Common misconceptions to listen for:

  • “A force is needed to keep an object moving.” Correct: unbalanced forces change motion; balanced forces do not change motion.
  • “Magnets attract all metals.” Correct: magnets attract things made of iron and some steels; most other metals, like aluminum foil and copper, do not stick.
  • “Forces only work when objects touch.” Correct: magnetic and static-electric forces can act without touching.
  • “A bigger push always makes an object go forever.” Correct: forces can change motion, but friction and other forces can slow objects.

Limits and cautions:

  • Gravity is not taught here; it moves to 5.2.
  • Simple machines are not a grade 3 expectation in this unit. They have their own optional lesson, 3.5 Simple Machines.
  • Static-electricity demos can fail on humid days; the provided question prompts and magnet investigation still count for the unit’s magnet standard.
  • Friction is simplified as a force that can slow motion. Deeper force models come in later grades.

Connections: Builds on: K-A Pushes and Pulls; Unit 0: How Science Works. Builds toward: 4.1 Energy, Speed, and Collisions; 5.2 Gravity, Stars, and Sky Patterns; Unit 3 Forces, Motion and Energy; Unit 8.1 Contact Forces and Collisions; Unit 8.3 Forces at a Distance.

After the lesson: activity

Play: Magnet sandbox

Drag the magnet around. Things that stick jump to the magnet. Things that do not stick stay still. Predict first: which things will jump? Write yes or no for each one before you test. Use the Reset button to start over.

Near you: Copper, like the copper from Michigan’s Upper Peninsula copper mines, does not stick. Petoskey stones, Michigan’s state stone, do not stick either.
